lines.text: Here's a web request handler, written in Python.

lines.text: It needs a user and that user's orders, so it asks two services at the same time, with async I O dot gather.
lines.caption: It needs a user and that user's orders, so it asks two services at the same time, with asyncio.gather.

lines.text: The user service takes one second.
lines.caption: The user service takes one second.

lines.caption: The orders service fails after a tenth of a second.

lines.caption: So the handler returns an error at a tenth of a second.

lines.text: But the request to the user service is still running.

lines.text: It finishes a full second after the request began, long after anyone was waiting for it.
lines.caption: It finishes a full second after the request began, long after anyone was waiting for it.

lines.caption: And if it had failed, its error would go nowhere.

lines.text: Each call has one way in and one way out.
lines.caption: Each call has one way in and one way out.

lines.caption: When fetch_user returns, it's finished.

lines.text: If it fails, the error comes back to the caller.
lines.caption: If it fails, the error comes back to the caller.

lines.text: And if the caller gives up, say the client hangs up, the server cancels it: it asks the code to stop, and the call it's waiting on stops too.
lines.caption: And if the caller gives up, say the client hangs up, the server cancels it: it asks the code to stop, and the call it's waiting on stops too.

lines.text: So when the handler returns, everything it started is done.

lines.text: Starting a task is different from calling a function.
lines.caption: Starting a task is different from calling a function.

lines.text: The start returns at once, and the task runs on by itself.
lines.caption: The start returns at once, and the task runs on by itself.

lines.text: Control splits into two paths, and nothing makes the second one come back.
lines.caption: Control splits into two paths, and nothing makes the second one come back.

lines.text: There are two common ways to wait for tasks, and both leave gaps.
lines.caption: There are two common ways to wait for tasks, and both leave gaps.

lines.text: The first is gather.
lines.caption: The first is gather.

lines.text: You'd expect it to behave like those calls.
lines.caption: You'd expect it to behave like those calls.

lines.text: It waits for both results, and when both requests succeed, it does.

lines.text: But when one fails, gather by default passes that error on immediately, and doesn't cancel the other task.
lines.caption: But when one fails, gather by default passes that error on immediately, and doesn't cancel the other task.

lines.text: The second way is to start both requests, then await them one at a time, the user request first.
lines.caption: The second way is to start both requests, then await them one at a time, the user request first.

lines.text: If the client gives up after half a second, the user request is cancelled, because it's the one being awaited.

lines.text: So a real fix has to do three things.
lines.caption: So a real fix has to do three things.

lines.text: Wait for every task it starts.

lines.caption: When one fails, cancel the rest and pass the error on.

lines.text: And when the caller gives up, cancel them all.

lines.text: This problem is older than concurrency.
lines.caption: This problem is older than concurrency.

lines.text: In 1968, Edsger Dike-stra argued against the go to statement.
lines.caption: In 1968, Edsger Dijkstra argued against the go to statement.

lines.text: With jumps that can lead anywhere, it becomes hard to follow what a program is doing from its text.
lines.caption: With jumps that can lead anywhere, it becomes hard to follow what a program is doing from its text.

lines.text: The fix was structured programming: blocks, conditionals, loops and function calls, where control goes in at the top and comes out at the bottom.
lines.caption: The fix was structured programming: blocks, conditionals, loops and function calls, where control goes in at the top and comes out at the bottom.

lines.text: Fifty years later, in 2018, Nathaniel Smith pointed out that starting a task is the same kind of jump.
lines.caption: Fifty years later, in 2018, Nathaniel Smith pointed out that starting a task is the same kind of jump.

lines.text: Control goes in, and part of it never has to come out, so you can no longer treat a function as a black box.
lines.caption: Control goes in, and part of it never has to come out, so you can no longer treat a function as a black box.

lines.text: His essay was called "Notes on structured concurrency, or: Go statement considered harmful".
lines.caption: His essay was called "Notes on structured concurrency, or: Go statement considered harmful".

lines.text: The fix is the same too: a block.
lines.caption: The fix is the same too: a block.

lines.text: Tasks started inside it can't outlive it.
lines.caption: Tasks started inside it can't outlive it.

lines.text: The block doesn't end until every task in it has finished.
lines.caption: The block doesn't end until every task in it has finished.

lines.text: That rule is called structured concurrency, a name Martin Sustrick had given it two years earlier.
lines.caption: That rule is called structured concurrency, a name Martin Sústrik had given it two years earlier.

lines.text: Smith built it into his own library, Trio, and Python's async I O later added the same kind of block, the task group, in version three point eleven.
